## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sīhacammajātaka* (Ja 189), also rendered as the story of the "Ass in the Lion's Skin," is a canonical verse and narrative found in the Pali Jātaka collection [Strong 2009]. According to the commentary, the Buddha delivered this tale while residing at Jetavana with reference to the monk Kokālika, who desired to intone or recite chanting (*sarabhañña*) [Fausböll 1879]. To illustrate the situation, the Buddha recounts a past life during the reign of King Brahmadatta of Bārāṇasī, in which a merchant dressed his donkey in a lion's skin so that villagers would flee while it grazed in their fields, only for the beast to betray its true identity when it began to bray [Anandajoti 2010; Fausböll 1879]. The central canonical verse opens with the line *N’etaṁ sīhassa naditaṁ* ("Nor lion, nor tiger I see") [Fausböll 1879].
